status: candidates — every entry pending human verification against its cited source before promotion
sourceMethod: Curated from the sourced sections of en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Albert_Camus (fetched 2026-07-17). All English translations of Camus are copyrighted; entries are short fair-use excerpts and the full texts are never ingested (see docs/source_strategy.md).

quotes.quote: Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday; I can't be sure.
quotes.note: French: 'Aujourd'hui, maman est morte. Ou peut-être hier, je ne sais pas.' Translations differ markedly — Matthew Ward's begins 'Maman died today.' The persona should note the translation when quoting.

quotes.quote: As if that great rush of anger had washed me clean, emptied me of hope … for the first time, the first, I laid my heart open to the benign indifference of the universe.
quotes.citation: The Stranger (1942), closing passage, Stuart Gilbert tr. (elided)
quotes.note: Matthew Ward renders it 'I opened myself to the gentle indifference of the world.'

quotes.quote: There is but one truly serious philosophical problem and that is suicide. Judging whether life is or is not worth living amounts to answering the fundamental question of philosophy.
quotes.citation: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), 'An Absurd Reasoning: Absurdity and Suicide,' opening

quotes.quote: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
quotes.citation: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), final lines
quotes.note: French: 'La lutte elle-même vers les sommets suffit à remplir un cœur d'homme; il faut imaginer Sisyphe heureux.'

quotes.quote: Happiness and the absurd are two sons of the same earth. They are inseparable.
quotes.citation: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), 'The Myth of Sisyphus'

quotes.quote: There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.
quotes.citation: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), 'The Myth of Sisyphus'

quotes.quote: What is a rebel? A man who says no.
Absolute freedom mocks at justice. Absolute justice denies freedom. To be fruitful, the two ideas must find their limits in each other.
quotes.citation: The Rebel (1951), 'Historical Murder,' Anthony Bower tr.

quotes.quote: The slave begins by demanding justice and ends by wanting to wear a crown.
Stupidity has a knack of getting its way; as we should see if we were not always so much wrapped up in ourselves.
God is not needed to create guilt or to punish. Our fellow men suffice, aided by ourselves.
In the depths of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer.
quotes.citation: 'Return to Tipasa' (1952/1954), as translated in Lyrical and Critical Essays (1968), p. 169
quotes.note: Frequently assumed to be an internet fabrication because of its greeting-card ubiquity — it is genuine. Useful in the opposite direction from most misattribution checks.

disputed.quote: Should I kill myself, or have a cup of coffee?
disputed.explanation: No documented occurrence in Camus's writings; traces to an uncited mention in Barry Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice. Likely falsely attributed.

disputed.quote: The only way to deal with an unfree world is to become so absolutely free that your very existence is an act of rebellion.
disputed.explanation: Found on quote sites, always without citation. No known source in Camus's works.

misattributions.quote: Don't walk behind me, I may not lead. Don't walk in front of me, I may not follow. Just walk beside me and be my friend.
misattributions.explanation: Widely attributed to Camus but apocryphal; researchers have searched his extant works without success (Quote Investigator, 2015). The wording is traceable to a children's song used at a Jewish summer camp, not to Camus.
misattributions.actualSource: A children's song used at a Jewish summer camp. Not Camus.
misattributions.verification: verified — corroborated by the live-search trap audit in docs/refactor_rag_scope_and_eval_harness_prompt.md (2026-07-23), which records the children's-song origin as confirmed.

misattributions.quote: There are causes worth dying for, but none worth killing for.
misattributions.explanation: Not Camus. The earliest occurrence of the sentiment on record is a 31 January 1943 letter by conscientious objector Albert Dietrich; the earliest attribution to Camus is an uncited 1999 quotation book. It also sits awkwardly with The Rebel's actual, more tragic treatment of violence.
misattributions.actualSource: Albert Dietrich, letter of 31 January 1943. Attribution to Camus first appears in an uncited 1999 quotation book.
misattributions.verification: verified — corroborated by the live-search trap audit in docs/refactor_rag_scope_and_eval_harness_prompt.md (2026-07-23), which dates the Dietrich letter and the 1999 attribution precisely.

misattributions.quote: Always go too far, because that's where you'll find the truth.
misattributions.explanation: No source in Camus's works; circulates unattributed on social media.

misattributions.quote: I think my life is of great importance, but I also think it is meaningless.
misattributions.explanation: Taken from Wikipedia's paraphrase of The Myth of Sisyphus's argument and mistaken for a quotation. Not Camus's sentence.

cautions.note: Camus explicitly and repeatedly rejected being called an existentialist ('No, I am not an existentialist' — interview in Les Nouvelles littéraires, 15 November 1945). The persona should resist the label and distinguish absurdism from Sartrean existentialism.
